title: Why Do Wheels Spin Backwards on Camera?
pause_note: 'long' lists beat indices followed by a 1.5 s pause

beats: Why do wheels spin backwards on camera?
A car speeds up on screen. Its wheels turn faster, then slow down, then stop, then start turning the wrong way, while the car keeps racing forward.
Helicopter blades can hang frozen in mid-air while the helicopter flies.
Nothing is wrong with the wheel, or with the camera. The trick is in what happens between the pictures.
And by the end, you will see why your own eyes, in the right light, can be fooled the same way.
Start with what a camera actually records.
It does not record motion. It records still pictures, one after another.
Cinema film shows twenty-four of them every second. Most video records twenty-five, thirty, or sixty.
Between two pictures, the camera sees little or nothing. Whatever happens in that gap, it simply misses.
Your brain fills the gap. It joins each picture to the next by guessing the shortest, simplest movement between them.
Psychologists call this apparent motion. It is the reason a flip book, or a film, looks alive at all.
Usually that guess is right. With a wheel, it can go badly wrong.
Here is a wagon wheel with twelve spokes. Every spoke looks exactly like every other.
Mark one of them in gold, just for us. The camera, and your brain, cannot see the mark.
Spin the wheel slowly. Between two frames it turns only a few degrees. Each spoke moves a little, and your brain matches each one with itself. Forward. Correct.
Now spin it faster. Between frames, each spoke now travels almost to where the next spoke was.
Your brain does not know which spoke is which. It sees a spoke just behind where one used to be, and picks the shortest move: a small step backwards.
The gold spoke went forward. The wheel you see went back.
Spin it a little faster still, so each spoke lands exactly where its neighbour was.
Every frame now looks identical to the one before. The wheel, turning at full speed, appears to stand perfectly still.
So the rule is simple. What matters is not how fast the wheel turns, but how far it turns between two frames, compared with the gap between two spokes.
Ignore whole gaps; only the leftover counts. Less than half a gap left over, and the wheel looks like it goes forward.
More than half a gap left over, and the nearest match is behind, so it looks like it runs backwards.
Exactly one whole gap, and it freezes.
For our twelve-spoke wheel at twenty-four frames a second, the gap between spokes is thirty degrees. Turn it two full times every second, and it freezes.
Engineers call this aliasing. A fast pattern, sampled too slowly, pretends to be a slower one.
To capture a repeating motion honestly, you need more than two samples per repeat. Fewer than that, and the samples lie.
Let's try a real car. Take a wheel with five spokes and a tyre about sixty-five centimetres tall, filmed at twenty-four frames a second.
That wheel looks frozen when each spoke moves exactly one gap per frame. Work it out, and that happens at about thirty-five kilometres an hour.
A little slower, and the wheel seems to crawl forward. A little faster, and it creeps backwards.
Speed up more, and the whole cycle repeats: forward, frozen, backwards, again and again as the car accelerates.
And the speed you see on screen has almost nothing to do with the real speed. A car at highway speed can show wheels creeping slowly backwards.
The same thing freezes helicopter rotors when their blades line up with the frames.
There is one more piece. Each frame is not an instant. The shutter stays open for a short time, and anything moving during that time smears.
A slow shutter blurs the spokes into a soft disc, and the illusion fades.
A fast shutter freezes each spoke crisply, and the illusion gets stronger.
So footage shot with very short exposures, like many phone clips in bright sun, shows it most clearly.
Next time you film a fan, a bike, or a car with your phone, watch the wheels.
Change the frame rate in your camera settings, and you can watch the wheel change direction.
But here is the strange part. People have seen wheels reverse with their own eyes, with no camera at all.
Some lights do the camera's job for it. Older fluorescent tubes and some cheap LED lamps flicker a hundred or a hundred and twenty times a second, too fast to notice.
Under them, a spinning wheel or a machine part is lit in flashes, just like frames. It can look slow, frozen, or reversed.
In factories this is a real danger. A lathe that looks stopped may be spinning at full speed.
Old record turntables used this on purpose. A ring of dots on the platter looks still under mains lighting when the speed is exactly right.
And stranger still, a few experiments report brief reversals even under steady, continuous light.
Some researchers think this means our vision takes snapshots of its own. Others think it is a contest between motion detectors in the brain. That question is still open.
So, why do wheels spin backwards on camera?
Because a camera sees in frames, and when the leftover step of each spoke between frames is more than halfway to the next one, your brain matches it to the wrong spoke.
The wheel goes forward. The pictures go backwards.
Have you ever caught a wheel or a fan doing this? Tell me where in the comments.
